headline_marked: [[JSON-to-Excel converters corrupt data]]: A 30-second test reveals silent errors in your spreadsheets.
headline: JSON-to-Excel converters corrupt data: A 30-second test reveals silent errors in your spreadsheets.
summary: Many popular JSON-to-Excel tools silently corrupt data, rounding large numbers, dropping leading zeros, or introducing formula injection risks without warning. A quick test can reveal if your data is safe.
details: Many online JSON-to-Excel converters silently corrupt data, leading to critical errors like incorrect order IDs or financial figures. This happens without any error messages, making the corrupted data appear perfectly valid.

The root cause lies in how JavaScript and Excel handle numbers. JavaScript's Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2⁵³−1) limits exact integer representation, causing larger numbers (like 64-bit database IDs) to be rounded by JSON.parse even before conversion.

Furthermore, Excel itself stores numbers as float64. Unless a converter explicitly writes large numbers or those with leading zeros as text, Excel will re-introduce rounding errors or drop leading zeros, affecting account numbers or PINs.

A significant security risk is formula injection. If a JSON value like "=1+1" or "=HYPERLINK(...)" is not treated as text, Excel can execute it upon opening, creating a vulnerability if the JSON originates from user input.

Dates can also be silently timezone-shifted by some tools, leading to incorrect values that are hard to detect. Developers are advised to run a simple 30-second test on any converter to verify its integrity.

A correct converter must preserve unsafe values (big IDs, leading zeros) as text while keeping clean numbers numeric for calculations. It should also guard against formula injection and leave dates untouched unless specified.

topic: ai agent fails real world test
headline_marked: [[AI-agent waste detector scored zero false positives]] in tests, then found a crack on a real trace
headline: AI-agent waste detector scored zero false positives in tests, then found a crack on a real trace
summary: A new AI-agent waste detector achieved zero false positives in synthetic tests, but revealed unexpected inefficiencies when applied to real-world traces. It targets redundant loops and re-queries to cut token costs.
details: The developer built Clew, a tool designed to find redundant loops, re-queries, and handoffs that silently burn tokens when multiple AI agents collaborate. It passed every synthetic test with zero false positives, but immediately found a "crack" when run on a real trace.

The original concept was failure prediction, using structural cycles in inter-agent message graphs and decay of novelty in embeddings. This approach, tested on UC Berkeley's MAST-Data (1,600+ multi-agent traces), failed to meet the success bar, primarily measuring trace length instead of failure.

The failure prediction experiment was shut down, deemed "unvalidated" but a win for providing a fast, honest answer. This experience became foundational, emphasizing the importance of designing experiments that are allowed to kill an idea quickly if it doesn't work.

An external IBM Research paper confirmed the correct approach: an unsupervised cycle-detection framework that processes structure first, then semantics. Their benchmark showed this cascade method achieved F1 0.72, significantly outperforming structure or semantics alone.

This insight shifted the project's focus from predicting failure to detecting redundant loops and handoffs that burn tokens, a more measurable and financially impactful problem. Strict, pre-registered GO/KILL criteria were established before any detection logic was written.

During calibration, a "fix" initially diversified data to hide a limitation where legitimate work was flagged as waste. The real solution routed the decision from the semantic layer to the structural layer, ensuring re-queries only counted if inputs were identical.

A pre-launch recall check identified a blind spot: one of four waste patterns (regenerative handoffs) scored 0/10. Rather than quietly remove it, the pattern was explicitly de-scoped, remaining in the dataset, and its misses counted against the aggregate F1 score.

Despite carrying this penalty, the single-shot evaluation returned a GO: F1 0.857, zero false positives, and 100% recall on the three in-scope patterns. Out-of-sample numbers precisely reproduced the dev numbers, confirming no overfitting to the development split.
